title: Given a binary array of zeros and ones, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of zeros and ones. Solve it with the prefix-sum and first-occurrence hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Contiguous Array (Longest Subarray with Equal Zeros and Ones)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array containing equally many zeros and ones. It is solved in linear time by treating each zero as minus one and each one as plus one, so that an equal-count subarray has a running sum of zero, then tracking a prefix sum and recording the first index at which each prefix value appears: the longest equal-count subarray spans between the first and the latest occurrence of any repeated prefix value.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a daily log of trade outcomes where one means a win and zero means a loss, and wants the longest continuous stretch where wins and losses exactly cancel out, a perfectly break-even run. He scores each win as plus one and each loss as minus one, keeps a running score, and remembers the earliest day each score first appeared. Whenever the running score returns to a value he has seen before, the stretch in between was perfectly break-even.
s1_definition.oneliner: Map zero to minus one, track the prefix sum, and the longest span between equal prefix values is the longest balanced subarray.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array containing equally many zeros and ones. It is solved in linear time by treating each zero as minus one and each one as plus one, so that an equal-count subarray has a running sum of zero, then tracking a prefix sum and recording the first index at which each prefix value appears: the longest equal-count subarray spans between the first and the latest occurrence of any repeated prefix value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a daily log of trade outcomes where one means a win and zero means a loss, and wants the longest continuous stretch where wins and losses exactly cancel out, a perfectly break-even run. He scores each win as plus one and each loss as minus one, keeps a running score, and remembers the earliest day each score first appeared. Whenever the running score returns to a value he has seen before, the stretch in between was perfectly break-even.

**One line to remember:** Map zero to minus one, track the prefix sum, and the longest span between equal prefix values is the longest balanced subarray.

sections.s2_technical:
The clever transformation is to replace every zero with minus one and keep every one as plus one. With that substitution, a subarray contains an equal number of zeros and ones exactly when its transformed sum is zero. And a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums, so a zero-sum subarray corresponds to two prefix sums that are equal. Therefore the longest balanced subarray is the longest distance between two indices that share the same prefix-sum value.

We maintain a running prefix sum, adding plus one for a one and minus one for a zero, and a hash map from a prefix-sum value to the first index at which it occurred. For each index, if the current prefix value has been seen before, the subarray from just after that first occurrence to the current index has a sum of zero, so its length is the current index minus the stored first-occurrence index, and we update the best length. If the prefix value is new, we store the current index as its first occurrence. Crucially we only ever store the first occurrence and never overwrite it, because the earliest occurrence gives the longest possible span to any later equal value.

The initialization that makes this correct is seeding the map with the prefix value zero mapped to index minus one, written `firstIndex.put(0, -1)`. This represents the empty prefix before the array starts, so that a balanced subarray beginning at index zero is measured correctly as current index minus minus one, which is current index plus one. The senior-level nuance is twofold: the minus-one-for-zero transformation that turns a counting problem into a zero-sum prefix problem, and the store-first-occurrence-only rule that guarantees maximal length.

Because the prefix values range only from minus the array length to plus the array length, a map keyed by integer works well. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass with constant-time map operations, and the space complexity is O(n) for the map. This transform-then-prefix technique is the standard pattern for equal-count and balance problems on binary data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a trading desk keeps a daily binary log of trade outcomes, one for a winning day and zero for a losing day, and risk management wants the longest continuous stretch in which wins and losses exactly balanced, a perfectly break-even run, because such runs are used to study periods of neutral strategy performance. This is exactly the contiguous-array equal-zeros-and-ones problem.

Problem 2 — Checking every possible stretch for balance by brute force is quadratic and too slow across the desk's long histories. The minus-one transformation combined with first-occurrence prefix tracking finds the longest balanced stretch in a single linear pass, which makes the neutral-performance analysis efficient.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `BreakEvenAnalyzer` service with a `longestBreakEvenRun` method implementing the transform-and-prefix approach, and a runnable `ContiguousArrayDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's win-loss logs, logging each balanced span found at fine level and the longest run at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's outcomes are 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0. We seed the first-index map with prefix 0 mapped to index minus one, start the prefix at 0, and the best at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 0: prefix becomes minus 1. It is new, so store prefix minus 1 at index 0.

Step 2 at index 1, value 1: prefix becomes 0. We have seen 0 before at index minus 1, so the balanced run spans index 0 to 1, length 1 minus minus 1 equals 2, best becomes 2.

Step 3 at index 2, value 0: prefix becomes minus 1. Seen before at index 0, so length is 2 minus 0 equals 2, best stays 2.

Step 4 at index 3, value 1: prefix becomes 0. Seen at index minus 1, length 3 minus minus 1 equals 4, best becomes 4.

Step 5 at index 4, value 1: prefix becomes 1. It is new, store prefix 1 at index 4.

Step 6 at index 5, value 0: prefix becomes 0. Seen at index minus 1, length 5 minus minus 1 equals 6, best becomes 6.

The longest break-even run for Rajesh is 6, the entire array, which has three ones and three zeros.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array with equally many zeros and ones, and I solve it in linear time with a transform-then-prefix-sum approach. The pivotal move is to treat every zero as minus one and every one as plus one, because then a subarray has equal counts exactly when its transformed sum is zero. Since a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums, a zero-sum subarray corresponds to two prefix sums that are equal, so the longest balanced subarray is the longest distance between two indices sharing the same prefix value.

I scan once, maintaining the running prefix and a map from each prefix value to the first index where it appeared. When the current prefix has been seen before, the subarray from just after that first occurrence to here is balanced, and I update the best length; when the prefix is new, I store the current index. The rule that makes this maximal is storing only the first occurrence and never overwriting it, because the earliest occurrence yields the longest span to any later equal value. I also seed the prefix value zero at index minus one so a balanced run starting at the very beginning measures correctly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on a trading desk. We kept a daily binary log of trade outcomes, one for a winning day and zero for a losing day, and risk management wanted the longest continuous stretch where wins and losses exactly balanced, a perfectly break-even run, to study periods of neutral strategy performance. The minus-one transformation plus first-occurrence prefix tracking found that longest balanced stretch in a single linear pass, scaling across the desk's long histories in the nightly analysis.

The senior-level point I make is that the minus-one-for-zero transformation is the insight that converts a counting problem into a zero-sum prefix problem, which is a reframing that unlocks the whole family of balance questions, and the store-first-occurrence-only rule is what guarantees the answer is maximal rather than just any balanced span. I also mention the seed of prefix zero at index minus one as the boundary detail that handles runs starting at index zero, and that the prefix range is bounded by the array length so an integer-keyed map or even an offset array works. Explaining the transformation, the first-occurrence rule, and the seeding together is what demonstrates to an interviewer that I truly understand the mechanics.
